# Beyond wrong answers: recovering links in Eedi's misconception graph

A wrong answer does not uniquely identify the reasoning that produced it. A student who adds the numerators and denominators of two fractions may have acquired an incorrect rule, but could also have made an accidental error. Distinguishing observations from hypotheses about cognition is central to education and behavior intervention.

We used Eedi's public knowledge graph to recover 3,308 held-out misconception-to-construct links. Graph retrieval achieved MAP@25 of 0.1500 versus 0.1413 for lexical retrieval, while lexical retrieval had better top-one accuracy. These are catalogue link recovery results, not measurements of student cognition.

![Experiment overview](/assets/research/h26-cover.svg)

## Learning from the competition

The [2024 Eedi Kaggle competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/eedi-mining-misconceptions-in-mathematics) asks systems to rank up to 25 misconceptions given a diagnostic question, correct answer and distractor. The [winning implementation](https://github.com/rbiswasfc/eedi-mining-misconceptions) uses Qwen-based retrieval and reranking alongside synthetic reasoning data inspired by novice learners and expert tutors. Retrieval limits the candidates requiring expensive reasoning. Generated rationales are not direct evidence of actual human mental states.

## Data and rights

[Eedi Misconceptions Graph v1.0](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Eedi/Eedi-Misconceptions-Graph), released in 2026 under CC BY 4.0, connects 8,117 misconceptions to 2,258 curriculum constructs through 19,294 edges. It excludes student responses, conversations, question text and images. We downloaded none of those records. We pinned revision fb9a4bedf17073a6e793822d7333b90f5a777ae6 and recorded the source hashes. The dataset's original edge weights describe the distribution of misconception taggings across constructs; we discarded those weights and used binary links.

## A measurable retrieval problem

![Training graph and held-out link](/assets/research/h26-method.svg)

We held out one existing edge per misconception with at least two links, using seed 2601. The remaining graph contains 15,986 edges. The 4,809 single-link misconceptions remain in the training graph but are excluded from evaluation. Thus the experiment does not measure performance on all misconceptions or entirely unseen nodes. For every query, observed edges are masked and the remaining constructs ranked. Ties are resolved by ascending construct ID.

Popularity ranks by training degree. Lexical retrieval computes word TF-IDF cosine similarity between misconception and construct names. Graph retrieval sums normalized construct co-occurrence similarities from the observed links. If A is the binary training adjacency matrix and d_j is construct j's degree, the similarity of distinct constructs j and k is (A transpose A)_jk / sqrt(d_j d_k). The removed edges never enter this computation. IDF uses the full public catalogue, making this a transductive known-node task rather than inductive learning.

With one held-out positive per query, AP@25 is reciprocal rank when the positive is within the first 25 results, and zero otherwise. MAP@25 averages that quantity across queries. Recall@25 reports whether the positive was retrieved; Top1 reports whether it was first.

## Measured results

![Measured retrieval metrics](/assets/research/h26-results.svg)

| Method | MAP@25 | Recall@25 | Top1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Popularity | 0.016281 | 7.26% | 0.70% |
| Lexical | 0.141316 | 37.12% | 8.25% |
| Graph | 0.150040 | 43.80% | 7.80% |

The graph method recovered 6.68 percentage points more targets within 25 results than lexical retrieval, but was 0.45 points worse at rank one. This suggests separating candidate generation and final ranking, not replacing lexical retrieval outright. All ranks and metrics matched on replay. A separate standard-library calculation verified the aggregate metrics; six unit tests check the evidence gate.

These results use one split of one catalogue. Shared nodes and dependence between queries limit generalization; neither multiple independent data sets nor an untouched external test were evaluated. They cannot be compared directly to Kaggle leaderboard scores.

## What this means for Manager

Rather than infer a single cause from one observation, a future behavior system should retrieve multiple plausible explanations, calibrate uncertainty, and update with authorized evidence. Interventions must respect the person's own goals and be evaluated against independent outcomes. Better catalogue retrieval establishes neither an accurate mental-state model nor a beneficial intervention.

No Manager weights or application code were changed in this study. Native competition reproduction, consented learner-turn analysis, independent evaluation and ManagerBench integration remain tracked in [issue #816](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/816). Learner-level data requires separate rights and safeguards, particularly for children.
